title: Nam Hoa Kinh (Trang Tử)
author: Zhuangzi (Trang Tử); dịch và chú giải: Nguyễn Hiến Lê
summary:
Nam Hoa Kinh is Nguyễn Hiến Lê's celebrated Vietnamese translation and commentary on the core writings attributed to Zhuangzi (Trang Tử, c. 4th century BCE), one of the two foundational figures of philosophical Taoism alongside Laozi. Nguyễn Hiến Lê, one of twentieth-century Vietnam's most prolific self-taught scholars and translators, approached the text not merely as a literal rendering but as an extended act of interpretation, supplying introductions, notes, and commentary intended to make a notoriously slippery, paradox-loving philosophical text accessible to a modern Vietnamese readership steeped more in Confucian than Taoist habits of thought. The book is built around what scholars generally regard as the most reliably authentic portion of the Zhuangzi corpus: the seven "Inner Chapters," believed most likely to reflect Zhuangzi's own voice, as distinct from the later Outer and Miscellaneous Chapters compiled by his followers.

The philosophical core of the work is a sustained argument against fixed, absolute standards of judgment — of right and wrong, big and small, useful and useless, life and death — in favor of a relativized, perspectival view in which every standpoint is valid only relative to the vantage point from which it is held. Zhuangzi illustrates this through some of the most famous images in Chinese philosophy: the giant Peng bird whose flight is incomprehensible to a small cicada and dove who mock its need for a long runway to take off; the butterfly dream, in which Zhuangzi wakes uncertain whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming he is a man; and the parable of the useless tree that survives precisely because its wood is worthless to loggers, subverting the ordinary assumption that usefulness is always a virtue.

Running alongside this relativism is Zhuangzi's ideal of the "true man" (chân nhân) or "free and easy wanderer" (tiêu dao), who has stopped clinging to social status, conventional achievement, or even the boundary between self and world, and instead moves through life with the effortless, unforced quality the Taoist tradition calls wu wei (vô vi). This is dramatized through figures like Cook Ding, whose knife glides through an ox's joints without ever striking bone because he has moved beyond mechanical technique into an intuitive harmony with the animal's natural structure — one of the text's most enduring images of mastery achieved by working with, rather than against, the grain of reality.

Nguyễn Hiến Lê's contribution is as much interpretive as translational: throughout the book he contextualizes Zhuangzi against Confucius and Laozi, flags where later commentators have disputed a passage's authenticity or meaning, and draws out the practical, almost therapeutic reading of Zhuangzi as an antidote to the anxious, status-driven Confucian ethic that dominated much of traditional Vietnamese and Chinese intellectual life. For readers encountering Zhuangzi for the first time through this edition, the effect is less a systematic philosophical treatise than an invitation to a different way of seeing — one that repeatedly undercuts its own claims to authority, in keeping with its argument that no single perspective, including its own, should be mistaken for the final truth.

sections.title: Tiêu Dao Du (Free and Easy Wandering)
sections.summary:
This opening chapter introduces Zhuangzi's central image of scale-dependent understanding through the story of the giant Peng bird, whose transformation from a fish of unimaginable size and its subsequent flight of thousands of miles is mocked by a small cicada and a dove, who cannot conceive of needing anything more than a short hop between trees. The chapter uses this to establish that judgments of "great" and "small," and by extension nearly all evaluative judgments, are relative to the limited horizon of the judge rather than objective facts about the world.

The middle of the chapter extends this into a broader meditation on freedom, contrasting people who are still bound by the need for external validation — fame, official position, the approval of a ruler — with the ideal of the "utterly free man" who has "no self," "no merit," and "no name," having let go of the categories by which ordinary people measure a worthwhile life. It includes the story of the ruler Yao offering to cede his throne to the recluse Xu You, who refuses on the grounds that he has no use for a title that would only obstruct his natural way of living, illustrating that true freedom is found by shedding ambition rather than achieving it.

The chapter closes with the parable of the huge, gnarled tree that a carpenter dismisses as useless because its wood cannot be worked, only for Zhuangzi to point out that this very uselessness is what allows the tree to grow undisturbed for centuries — planting a theme of "usefulness in uselessness" that recurs throughout the later Inner Chapters.
keyLessons: Judgments of scale and worth are relative to the limited perspective of the one making them, not objective facts.
Freedom is achieved by releasing the need for external validation, not by acquiring more status or achievement.
What looks like uselessness by conventional standards can be exactly what protects something from being consumed or destroyed.

sections.title: Tề Vật Luận (On the Equality of Things)
sections.summary:
This chapter is the philosophical heart of the Inner Chapters, opening with the image of "the piping of heaven" — the wind passing through the countless different hollows of a mountain forest, each producing a different sound, none of which is more "correct" than another, used as a metaphor for the endless variety of human opinions, each sincerely felt yet none possessing final authority. From here the chapter builds its sustained argument that the fierce debates between rival philosophical schools (particularly the Confucians and Mohists) over what is right and wrong are ultimately disputes between equally partial perspectives, neither of which can step outside itself to adjudicate the other.

The chapter's most famous passage is the butterfly dream: Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, flitting about with no awareness of being Zhuangzi, then wakes with a start to find himself unmistakably Zhuangzi again — yet is left unable to say with certainty whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he is a man, illustrating the porousness of the boundary between waking judgment and dream, self and other, that the chapter's relativism ultimately implies.

The chapter concludes by extending this relativizing logic even to life and death themselves, suggesting that our fear of death may be as misplaced as a captive weeping at first over being taken from home, only to later regret ever wanting to leave — proposing that we cannot know from within life whether death is truly the loss we assume it to be.
keyLessons: Rival claims to absolute truth are often equally partial perspectives that cannot adjudicate each other from a neutral standpoint.
The boundary we assume between dream and waking, self and other, is less solid than ordinary consciousness suggests.
Fear of death rests on an assumption about its nature that we have no actual grounds to confirm.

sections.title: Dưỡng Sinh Chủ (The Secret of Caring for Life)
sections.summary:
This short but pivotal chapter introduces the ideal of preserving one's vital energy by avoiding both reckless indulgence and rigid, exhausting striving after either virtue or fame, since both extremes wear down the life-force the chapter is concerned with nurturing. It sets up its central teaching through the famous story of Cook Ding butchering an ox for Lord Wenhui: after nineteen years, his knife remains as sharp as the day it was forged because he no longer hacks mechanically at bone and sinew but follows the natural openings and structure of the animal, letting the blade glide through where there is already space.

The chapter uses Lord Wenhui's astonished reaction to draw out the lesson explicitly: Cook Ding explains that he no longer "looks" at the ox with his eyes but engages it with his spirit, moving according to the natural grain of things rather than forcing his way through by strength — an image of mastery achieved not through more effort but through deeper attunement.

The chapter closes with two brief additional images — a one-legged man who has made peace with his condition, and the death of a well-regarded teacher whose passing his friend mourns only lightly, on the grounds that clinging to grief is itself a way of resisting the natural course of things — reinforcing that the chapter's ideal of "caring for life" is ultimately about working with nature's rhythms rather than fighting them.
keyLessons: Genuine mastery in any skill comes from working with the underlying structure of a situation rather than forcing one's way through it by effort alone.
Wearing yourself out chasing either excessive virtue or excessive gain both threaten the same vital energy.
Accepting the natural course of loss and change preserves more inner peace than resisting it.

sections.title: Nhân Gian Thế (In the Human World)
sections.summary:
This chapter turns from personal cultivation to the perilous business of living and working among other people, particularly those in positions of power. It opens with Confucius (used here, as often in the Zhuangzi, as a mouthpiece for ideas not strictly Confucian) counseling a disciple against rushing to remonstrate with a tyrannical ruler, warning that moral righteousness alone, without tact and self-preservation, tends to get reformers killed rather than heeded.

The middle of the chapter develops the theme of "the fasting of the mind" (tâm trai) — a practice of emptying oneself of preconceptions and ego-driven agendas so as to respond to a difficult situation, and a difficult ruler, with genuine adaptability rather than a fixed plan that a hostile audience will simply reject. It returns again to the motif of "the useless tree," this time an enormous oak venerated as a shrine tree, whose very uselessness for lumber has let it survive for centuries where more "useful" trees were cut down long ago.

The chapter closes with the image of the madman of Chu singing a song to Confucius about the dangers of being too visibly capable in a chaotic age — "the useful tree is cut down first" — tying the chapter's practical advice about surviving political life back to the recurring theme that visible usefulness invites danger, while apparent uselessness can be a form of protection.
keyLessons: Moral righteousness without tact and timing often gets a reformer destroyed rather than heard.
Emptying oneself of fixed agendas allows for more genuine, adaptive responses to difficult people and situations.
In a dangerous or competitive environment, being conspicuously the most capable or useful person can itself become a liability.

sections.title: Đức Sung Phù (The Sign of Virtue Complete)
sections.summary:
This chapter gathers a series of stories about people with severe physical deformities or mutilations — men missing a foot, a grotesquely ugly man whom everyone nonetheless wants to be near — who nonetheless possess such complete inner virtue and equanimity that others are drawn to them regardless of appearance. It argues that true "virtue" (đức) in the Taoist sense has nothing to do with physical wholeness or conventional attractiveness, but is instead a quality of inner stillness and acceptance that radiates outward.

The chapter's key exchange is between Confucius and a one-footed man named Wang Tai, whose students rival Confucius's own in number despite his disability and his refusal to teach in any conventional sense; Confucius explains to a skeptical follower that Wang Tai has achieved a state of mind so settled and undisturbed by loss that people are drawn to the stillness itself, not to anything he actively does or says.

The chapter closes by explicitly contrasting outer physical completeness with inner virtue's completeness, arguing that a person who has integrated loss and change without resentment has achieved something far rarer and more admirable than ordinary physical wholeness — reframing what conventional society treats as misfortune as, at times, closer to spiritual advantage.
keyLessons: Inner stillness and genuine acceptance of one's circumstances can draw people more powerfully than physical wholeness or conventional charisma.
What society labels as misfortune does not necessarily correlate with a diminished inner life.
Teaching by embodiment and presence can be more powerful than teaching by active instruction.

sections.title: Đại Tông Sư (The Great and Venerable Teacher)
sections.summary:
This chapter turns to the nature of the Tao itself and the ideal of the "True Man" (chân nhân) who has fully realized it — someone who does not fear death, does not cling to life, accepts both gain and loss with equal composure, and moves through the world's transformations the way the seasons move through the year, without resistance. It includes some of the text's most direct statements about death as simply one more transformation in an endless natural process, no more to be feared than any other change of form.

The chapter's most vivid illustration is the story of four friends who agree that whoever falls ill or dies first, the others will simply watch and learn from the process rather than grieve; when one friend's body twists and deforms from illness, he marvels at what strange new form the "Creator" might make of him next, treating his own bodily disintegration with curiosity rather than dread.

The chapter closes with a related story of friends attending a funeral who instead sing and play music, scandalizing a visiting disciple of Confucius, only for the deeper point to emerge that these men understand life and death as a single continuous process rather than two separate, opposed states — the chapter's fullest statement of the equanimity the whole book has been building toward.
keyLessons: Accepting death as simply another transformation, rather than an opposite of life, can dissolve much of the fear surrounding it.
Watching one's own decline or misfortune with curiosity rather than resistance is presented as a genuine, achievable stance, not mere resignation.
Social rituals around loss (like conventional mourning) are themselves relative customs, not the only valid response to death.

sections.title: Ứng Đế Vương (Fit to Be Emperors and Kings)
sections.summary:
The final Inner Chapter turns to the implications of Zhuangzi's philosophy for governance, arguing that the best ruler governs by wu vi — non-interference — allowing people and affairs to follow their own natural course rather than imposing constant active management, in implicit contrast to the more interventionist, ritual-and-hierarchy-driven Confucian model of statecraft.

Its most famous passage is the parable of Hundun ("Chaos"), a formless being who hosts two other rulers, Shu and Hu, who decide to repay his hospitality by drilling seven holes into him — the openings that other beings use to see, hear, eat, and breathe — reasoning that he alone lacks them; Hundun dies on the seventh day, once the last hole is bored. The story functions as a warning against imposing well-intentioned "improvement" or standardized structure onto something whose nature is fundamentally different, killing the very thing the improvers meant to help.

The chapter, and the Inner Chapters as a whole, close on this cautionary note, using the death of Hundun to crystallize the entire book's argument: that forcing a single fixed standard — of goodness, usefulness, or "proper" form — onto a world of naturally varied and self-sufficient things tends to destroy rather than improve what it touches.
keyLessons: Effective leadership often means allowing people and situations to unfold according to their own nature rather than constantly intervening.
Well-intentioned attempts to "improve" something according to an external standard can destroy the very thing that made it work.
Respecting a system's or a person's own internal logic is often wiser than imposing a uniform structure from outside.
Judgments of big and small, useful and useless, right and wrong are relative to the perspective from which they are made, not fixed facts about the world.
Genuine mastery of a skill comes from attunement to a situation's natural structure, not from forcing one's way through by sheer effort.
Visible ambition and conspicuous usefulness can attract danger in a competitive or hierarchical environment; apparent uselessness can be protective.
Moral conviction without tact and timing frequently destroys the reformer rather than achieving reform.
Inner stillness and acceptance draw people and hold influence more durably than outward achievement or physical wholeness.
Treating death as one more natural transformation, rather than life's opposite, is presented as a route to genuine equanimity.
The best kind of governance, and the best kind of help, often consists of stepping back rather than intervening.
No single perspective, including the reader's own settled convictions, should be mistaken for the final, complete truth.

whoThisIsFor: Readers drawn to Eastern philosophy, anyone feeling burned out by achievement-oriented thinking, and readers of Nguyễn Hiến Lê's other self-cultivation and classical-thought translations looking for a more contemplative counterpart.
whenToReadThis: Best read slowly, ideally alongside a period of reflection or transition, rather than as a quick reference — the text rewards rereading individual parables more than linear cover-to-cover consumption.

authorBio.name: Zhuangzi (Trang Tử) — original author; Nguyễn Hiến Lê — translator and commentator
authorBio.bio:
Zhuangzi (莊子, c. 369–286 BCE) was a Chinese philosopher of the Warring States period and, alongside Laozi, one of the two foundational figures of philosophical Taoism. Little reliable biographical detail survives about his life beyond scattered anecdotes, some likely apocryphal, describing him as a minor official who declined offers of high office in favor of a life of contemplative independence. His name is attached to the text that bears it, the Zhuangzi, though modern scholarship generally attributes only the seven "Inner Chapters" to Zhuangzi himself, with the remaining Outer and Miscellaneous Chapters understood to be later additions by his followers and other Taoist-adjacent writers.

Nguyễn Hiến Lê (1912–1984) was one of twentieth-century Vietnam's most prolific self-taught scholars, translators, and essayists, publishing roughly 120 works across self-cultivation, history, biography, linguistics, and translations of major Chinese and Western philosophical texts over a writing career based mainly in Saigon (later Long Xuyên) from the 1950s through the 1980s. Known for a disciplined, almost monastic daily writing and research routine, he built a reputation as both a popularizer of classical Chinese thought for Vietnamese readers and an advocate of rigorous self-education, notably declining Vietnam's National Literature Prize for translation in 1970 on grounds of maintaining his intellectual independence.

His Nam Hoa Kinh translation and commentary is considered one of the standard Vietnamese-language entry points to Zhuangzi, valued particularly for the clarity of its explanatory notes situating the text against Confucian and Legalist thought of the same period.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Wu Vi (Vô Vi / Non-Action)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The central Taoist ideal of acting in effortless accordance with the natural course of things rather than through forced, willful intervention. It does not mean literal passivity but rather a mode of action so well attuned to a situation's own structure that it requires no strain — exemplified by Cook Ding's knife gliding through the ox.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Tề Vật (The Equality/Leveling of Things)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Zhuangzi's central relativist thesis that apparently opposed categories — big and small, right and wrong, self and other, life and death — are equally valid only from within a particular limited perspective, and that no vantage point can claim final, absolute authority over the others.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Tâm Trai (The Fasting of the Mind)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A practice of deliberately emptying the mind of fixed preconceptions, ego-driven agendas, and rigid plans so as to respond to people and circumstances with genuine adaptability, introduced in the chapter on living safely amid the dangers of human society.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Chân Nhân (The True Man / Realized Person)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Zhuangzi's ideal figure, who has achieved such complete acceptance of life's transformations — including death — that they move through gain, loss, praise, and blame with unshaken equanimity, exemplified by the friends in the "Great and Venerable Teacher" chapter who greet illness and death with curiosity rather than fear.

actionSteps: The next time you find yourself in a heated disagreement over what is "clearly" right, deliberately try to state the other side's position as persuasively as you can from within their own perspective, before responding — practicing the book's relativist lens directly.

In a skill you are trying to improve, spend one practice session paying attention only to the natural "grain" of the task (timing, rhythm, structure) rather than pushing harder, in the spirit of Cook Ding's knife.

Identify one situation in your life where you are being conspicuously "useful" or visible in a way that is creating pressure or risk for you, and experiment with deliberately stepping back for a defined period.

Before your next attempt to fix, improve, or reform something (a process, a relationship, a team), pause and ask whether the thing's own internal logic is actually broken, or whether your standard for "proper" form is simply different from its natural one — in the spirit of the Hundun parable.

Write down one loss, decline, or ending you are currently resisting, and try describing it for a few minutes the way the friends in "Đại Tông Sư" describe illness — as a transformation to observe with curiosity rather than a misfortune to fight.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your life have you mistaken a perspective that feels obviously true to you for an objective, universal fact?
Is there an area of your life where being conventionally "useful" or high-achieving has actually put you at greater risk or under greater strain than staying less visible would have?
What would it mean, practically, for you to care for one relationship or responsibility in your life with less forced effort and more attunement to its natural rhythm?

points: The Zhuangzi corpus, even in its Inner Chapters, is understood by most scholars to be an edited, composite text passed through centuries of oral and written transmission before its final compilation under the editor Guo Xiang (郭象) around the 3rd century CE, meaning the "authentic Zhuangzi voice" a reader encounters has already been shaped by centuries of later hands.

Zhuangzi's relativism, taken to its logical extreme, risks self-undermining: if no perspective can claim authority over another, it is unclear on what basis the text's own claims (including the claim of relativism itself) should be accepted as more insightful than any other view — a tension noted by many commentators on the text across centuries.

The philosophy's emphasis on acceptance and non-striving, while offering real psychological relief from anxious over-achievement, can in less careful readings tip into a rationale for passivity or disengagement from genuinely fixable problems and injustices.

As with any translation of classical Chinese philosophical text, Nguyễn Hiến Lê's Vietnamese rendering necessarily involves interpretive choices about famously ambiguous passages; readers seeking the most literal possible meaning should cross-reference with other translations or the original classical Chinese.
criticalTake.contextNote: Zhuangzi's ideas have aged unusually well as a counterpoint to modern productivity and achievement culture, and are frequently cited in contemporary discussions of burnout, acceptance, and flow states, even by readers with no interest in Taoism as a religious tradition.

sourceNotes: The philosophical content, chapter structure, and quotations in this entry are based on general, well-established scholarly and popular knowledge of the Zhuangzi's seven Inner Chapters (Tiêu Dao Du, Tề Vật Luận, Dưỡng Sinh Chủ, Nhân Gian Thế, Đức Sung Phù, Đại Tông Sư, Ứng Đế Vương), which are widely and consistently documented across translations and commentary. Quotations are given as commonly rendered paraphrases of well-known, frequently cited passages rather than verified against Nguyễn Hiến Lê's specific Vietnamese wording, since the exact text of his particular translation could not be directly accessed for word-for-word verification; readers wanting his precise Vietnamese phrasing should check against the physical book. Nguyễn Hiến Lê's biographical details are drawn from general, widely corroborated Vietnamese literary-history sources found via web search.
